structuredClone does a real deep copy that keeps Date, Map, Set, typed arrays, undefined, NaN/Infinity, BigInt and circular references, while the JSON round trip turns Dates into strings, drops undefined and functions, mangles NaN, and throws on cycles. structuredClone throws on functions and DOM nodes, and neither keeps class prototypes. Use structuredClone unless you specifically want a JSON-safe copy.

`docker compose up -d` creates containers (and networks/volumes) if they don't exist, recreates them if their config or image changed, and starts them in the background. `docker compose start` only starts containers that already exist and are stopped, with no creation or config changes, and errors if there are none. For our local setup, `docker compose up -d db redis` is the one to use.

AsyncLocalStorage gives you per-request context (request id, user, tracing) that follows async calls without threading it through every function argument. It's cheap enough that the overhead is usually negligible next to I/O, though it isn't free and the cost depends on the Node version, so measure if it's on a very hot path. It would fit the requestId problem we were just looking at.

A Deployment treats pods as interchangeable and stateless: any pod can be replaced or scaled in any order. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable name (name-0, name-1), stable DNS, its own persistent volume that sticks to it, and ordered start/stop and rolling updates. Pick it when identity or per-pod storage matters, like databases, Kafka or Zookeeper-style clusters.
